The Maestro · Part 6 · Phase 1 · 🏗️ Infrastructure hat

Day Zero: Bring-Up

The 128 nodes arrive in month 3. On paper they are identical; in practice some will have a loose cable, a GPU with failing memory, an old firmware version or a fabric port running at half speed. Any one of them can slow or stop a job that uses all 1,024 GPUs. Bring-up is the work of finding them before the training run does. This part is Gopala's day-zero runbook: what to check on each node, how to test the network in pairs and as a whole, how to read NCCL bandwidth numbers, a small parser that flags bad pairs, and the acceptance report that starts the bill.

1. Mission log: weeks 13–18

Week 13 · First 32 nodes
  • The provider delivers a quarter of the block early (Part 4). Gopala runs the per-node burn-in (section 6) and parks every failing node.
Weeks 14–16 · Network
  • Runs pairwise and full-fabric NCCL tests (sections 5–7) as more nodes arrive; finds and reports bad links.
Weeks 17–18 · Acceptance
  • The full 128 nodes pass the contract acceptance test (Part 4) after replacements; billing starts. Maestro-0 post-training begins on the first accepted nodes.

2. Why trust nothing

Why trust nothing: Llama 3 405B, 54 days

466job interruptions
419unexpected
30.1%of unexpected: faulty GPUs
17.2%of unexpected: GPU HBM3 memory

Meta, The Llama 3 Herd of Models (16,384 H100s).

  • Large training runs fail mostly because of hardware.
    • Meta's Llama 3 paper is the clearest public record: in a 54-day snapshot of pre-training Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100s, there were 466 job interruptions, 419 of them unexpected.
    • Faulty GPUs caused 30.1% of the unexpected ones and GPU HBM3 memory 17.2%
      • network switches and cables, host maintenance, SRAM, system processors and others made up the rest.
    • Meta still reached more than 90% effective training time, because it found and replaced bad parts fast.
  • Gopala's cluster is 16 times smaller, so he should expect roughly 16 times fewer failures per day (Part 7 does the arithmetic), but the first weeks are the worst: parts that are going to fail early ("infant mortality") do so under the first sustained load.
    • Bring-up means applying that load deliberately, before his job depends on it.
  • The site's Who Runs the AI Factory:
    • bring-up and firmware article covers the roles and tools at hyperscale
    • this part is the hands-on version for one person and 128 nodes.

5. Before the OS: inventory through the BMC

  • Every server has a baseboard management controller (BMC): a small computer on the motherboard that can power the node on and off, read its sensors and report its hardware and firmware, even when no operating system is installed.
    • Modern BMCs speak Redfish, the DMTF's standard REST API, so one script can inventory servers from different vendors.

Gopala uses it on day zero to compare every node against the expected configuration before spending an hour installing anything:

redfish_inventory.py · Python 3, no dependencies; runs against a built-in mock BMC
"""redfish_inventory.py — inventory nodes through their BMCs (DMTF Redfish)
and flag firmware drift before anything boots an OS.

Redfish is the standard REST API of server baseboard management
controllers: /redfish/v1/Systems, /Chassis, /UpdateService/FirmwareInventory.
Run with no arguments, it starts a small MOCK BMC (three fake nodes) in a
thread and inventories that, so the code path can be checked without
hardware. On a real cluster: python3 redfish_inventory.py bmc1 bmc2 ...
(add authentication and TLS verification for real BMCs).
"""
import json, sys, threading, urllib.request
from collections import Counter
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

MOCK = {  # node -> (serial, BIOS, BMC firmware, GPU VBIOS, NIC firmware, health)
    "node001": ("SN-1001", "1.4.2", "24.09", "96.00.99.00.01", "28.42.1000", "OK"),
    "node002": ("SN-1002", "1.4.2", "24.09", "96.00.99.00.01", "28.42.1000", "OK"),
    "node003": ("SN-1003", "1.3.7", "24.09", "96.00.99.00.01", "28.39.1002", "Warning"),
}

class BMC(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): pass
    def do_GET(self):
        node, path = self.path.split("/", 2)[1], "/" + self.path.split("/", 2)[2]
        sn, bios, bmc, vb, nic, health = MOCK[node]
        if path == "/redfish/v1/Systems/1":
            body = {"SerialNumber": sn, "BiosVersion": bios, "Status": {"Health": health},
                    "ProcessorSummary": {"Count": 2}, "MemorySummary": {"TotalSystemMemoryGiB": 2048}}
        elif path == "/redfish/v1/UpdateService/FirmwareInventory":
            body = {"Members": [{"Id": "BMC", "Version": bmc}, {"Id": "GPU_VBIOS", "Version": vb},
                                {"Id": "NIC", "Version": nic}]}
        else:
            self.send_response(404); self.end_headers(); return
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(data)

def get(base, path):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(base + path, timeout=5) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def inventory(base):
    s = get(base, "/redfish/v1/Systems/1")
    fw = {m["Id"]: m["Version"] for m in get(base, "/redfish/v1/UpdateService/FirmwareInventory")["Members"]}
    return {"serial": s["SerialNumber"], "health": s["Status"]["Health"], "BIOS": s["BiosVersion"], **fw}

def main():
    if sys.argv[1:]:
        targets = {h: f"https://{h}" for h in sys.argv[1:]}
    else:
        srv = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), BMC)
        threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
        targets = {n: f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_port}/{n}" for n in MOCK}
    inv = {n: inventory(b) for n, b in targets.items()}
    keys = ["BIOS", "BMC", "GPU_VBIOS", "NIC"]
    print(f"{'node':8s} {'serial':8s} {'health':8s} " + " ".join(f"{k:15s}" for k in keys))
    for n, r in inv.items():
        print(f"{n:8s} {r['serial']:8s} {r['health']:8s} " + " ".join(f"{r[k]:15s}" for k in keys))
    for k in keys:
        golden, _ = Counter(r[k] for r in inv.values()).most_common(1)[0]
        odd = [n for n, r in inv.items() if r[k] != golden]
        if odd:
            print(f"DRIFT {k}: golden {golden}, different on {', '.join(odd)}")
    sick = [n for n, r in inv.items() if r["health"] != "OK"]
    print("hold back before OS install:", ", ".join(sorted(set(sick + [n for k in keys for n, r in inv.items()
          if r[k] != Counter(x[k] for x in inv.values()).most_common(1)[0][0]]))) or "none")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 redfish_inventory.py # three mock nodes, not real hardware node serial health BIOS BMC GPU_VBIOS NIC node001 SN-1001 OK 1.4.2 24.09 96.00.99.00.01 28.42.1000 node002 SN-1002 OK 1.4.2 24.09 96.00.99.00.01 28.42.1000 node003 SN-1003 Warning 1.3.7 24.09 96.00.99.00.01 28.39.1002 DRIFT BIOS: golden 1.4.2, different on node003 DRIFT NIC: golden 28.42.1000, different on node003 hold back before OS install: node003
  • The run above is real but the "BMC" is a small mock server the script starts itself, with node003 deliberately given an older BIOS and NIC firmware and a warning status, so the drift logic can be seen working.
    • Against real BMCs the same code reads the same paths (/redfish/v1/Systems and /redfish/v1/UpdateService/FirmwareInventory), with authentication and certificate checks added
      • exact resource names vary by vendor, so the first real run is checked by hand.
  • Why bother before the OS?
    • Because firmware drift is cheap to fix before a node is in service and expensive after: a node with an older NIC firmware can pass every single-node test and only misbehave in a 1,024-GPU collective, where it is hardest to find.

6. The per-node burn-in

  • One script per node, run in parallel across the delivered nodes.
    • Every step either passes or keeps the node out of the pool; there is no "mostly fine".
    • Logs go to a shared directory so every result is kept with the node's serial numbers.
burnin.sh · needs a real 8-GPU node · not executed for this article
#!/bin/bash
# burnin.sh NODE — day-zero acceptance for one 8-GPU node.
# Every step must pass; any failure keeps the node out of the pool.
set -euo pipefail
N=$1; LOG=/acceptance/$N; mkdir -p $LOG
run() { echo "== $1"; ssh $N "$2" > $LOG/$1.log 2>&1 || { echo "FAIL $1 on $N"; exit 1; }; }

run inventory  "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,serial,vbios_version,memory.total --format=csv"
run firmware   "nvidia-smi -q | grep -E 'VBIOS|Inforom' ; ibstat | grep -E 'Firmware|Rate'"
run topology   "nvidia-smi topo -m"                 # 8 GPUs on NVSwitch, NICs on the right PCIe roots
run ecc        "nvidia-smi -q -d ECC | grep -E 'Pending|Uncorr'"
run dcgm_long  "dcgmi diag -r 3"                    # memory, PCIe, NVLink, stress (~30-60 min)
run ib_links   "ibstat | grep -c 'State: Active'"   # expect one per compute NIC
run nccl_local "all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 8G -f 2 -g 8"   # NVLink only, single node
run burn_24h   "dcgmi diag -r 4 || gpu_burn 86400"      # thermals under sustained load
grep -q "Fail" $LOG/dcgm_long.log && { echo "FAIL dcgm on $N"; exit 1; }
echo "PASS $N"

Notes on the choices:

  • DCGM level 3 is NVIDIA's long diagnostic (memory, PCIe bandwidth, NVLink, targeted stress); level 4 adds longer tests. They take from tens of minutes to hours, which is why nodes are tested in parallel.
  • The single-node all-reduce checks NVLink and NVSwitch inside the node before the network is involved, so a bad result points to the node, not the fabric.
  • The 24-hour burn exists to trigger early failures and thermal problems. It is expensive in time, but it is cheaper than losing a day of a 1,024-GPU run.

7. Reading NCCL numbers

  • nccl-tests prints two bandwidths.
    • algbw is data size divided by time.
    • busbw rescales it so the number can be compared with the hardware's link speed, whatever the number of GPUs: for all-reduce, busbw = algbw × 2(n−1)/n, where n is the number of ranks.
    • For 16 GPUs (two nodes) the factor is 1.875; for 1,024 GPUs it is almost exactly 2.
  • What is "good"?
    • Inside one H100 node, NVLink gives each GPU up to 900 GB/s total.
    • Between nodes, each GPU has its own 400 Gb/s NIC, i.e. 50 GB/s per direction, so the inter-node bus bandwidth for large messages is bounded by the network, not NVLink.
    • The exact achievable figure depends on the NCCL version, topology and settings, so Gopala does not compare against a number from the internet: he compares nodes with each other, and the trial cluster with the contract figure.
    • A pair far below its peers is a defect, whatever the absolute number.

9. Testing in pairs, and a parser

Pairwise NCCL bus bandwidth (sample log)

node001 + node002356 GB/s
node003 + node004354 GB/s
node005 + node006164 GB/s ✗
node007 + node008355 GB/s

Real output of nccl_check.py on a sample log written for this article, not a real cluster.

  • A full-cluster test tells him whether the whole is slow, not where.
    • So he first runs 2-node tests on all pairs in a pattern (node 1 with 2, 3 with 4, and so on, then shifted), and the parser below flags any pair below 90% of the best.
    • A node that is in two flagged pairs is the suspect; it is drained and tested alone.
nccl_check.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""nccl_check.py — read nccl-tests all_reduce_perf output and flag bad nodes.

Usage: python3 nccl_check.py [log ...]. With no file it parses SAMPLE,
a log written for this article in the nccl-tests format (not from a real
cluster) so the parser and the maths can be checked.
"""
import re, sys

# Pairwise 2-node runs (16 GPUs): node pair -> busbw at 8 GB messages.
SAMPLE = """\
# pair node001,node002
  8589934592    2147483648     float     sum      -1  45210  190.00  356.25      0
# pair node003,node004
  8589934592    2147483648     float     sum      -1  45480  188.87  354.13      0
# pair node005,node006
  8589934592    2147483648     float     sum      -1  98120   87.54  164.14      0
# pair node007,node008
  8589934592    2147483648     float     sum      -1  45390  189.24  354.83      0
"""
ROW = re.compile(r"^\s*(\d+)\s+(\d+)\s+\w+\s+\w+\s+-?\d+\s+([\d.]+)\s+([\d.]+)\s+([\d.]+)\s+(\d+)")

def busbw_factor(n):
    # all-reduce moves 2(n-1)/n of the data per rank (nccl-tests PERFORMANCE.md)
    return 2 * (n - 1) / n

def parse(text):
    out, pair = [], None
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("# pair"):
            pair = line.split()[2]
        m = ROW.match(line)
        if m and pair:
            size, t_us, alg, bus, wrong = int(m[1]), float(m[3]), float(m[4]), float(m[5]), int(m[6])
            out.append((pair, size, t_us, alg, bus, wrong))
    return out

def main():
    text = "".join(open(f).read() for f in sys.argv[1:]) if sys.argv[1:] else SAMPLE
    rows = parse(text)
    n = 16
    f = busbw_factor(n)
    print(f"ranks={n}: busbw = algbw x {f:.4f}")
    best = max(r[4] for r in rows)
    for pair, size, t, alg, bus, wrong in rows:
        alg_calc = size / (t * 1e-6) / 1e9
        flag = "OK" if bus >= 0.9 * best and wrong == 0 else "SUSPECT"
        print(f"{pair:18s} algbw {alg:6.2f} (recalc {alg_calc:6.2f}) busbw {bus:6.2f} GB/s "
              f"x{f:.4f}={alg*f:6.2f}  {flag}")
    bad = [r[0] for r in rows if r[4] < 0.9 * best]
    print("drain and re-test individually:", ", ".join(bad) if bad else "none")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 nccl_check.py # on the built-in sample log ranks=16: busbw = algbw x 1.8750 node001,node002 algbw 190.00 (recalc 190.00) busbw 356.25 GB/s x1.8750=356.25 OK node003,node004 algbw 188.87 (recalc 188.87) busbw 354.13 GB/s x1.8750=354.13 OK node005,node006 algbw 87.54 (recalc 87.55) busbw 164.14 GB/s x1.8750=164.14 SUSPECT node007,node008 algbw 189.24 (recalc 189.25) busbw 354.83 GB/s x1.8750=354.83 OK drain and re-test individually: node005,node006
  • The parser also recomputes algbw from the message size and time and the busbw factor from the rank count, so a misread column or a mislabelled run shows up immediately.
    • On a real cluster it reads one log per pair: python3 nccl_check.py logs/pair_*.txt.
  • After the pairs pass, the full 1,024-GPU run is the final test.
    • Its bus bandwidth should be close to the pair results
      • if it falls well below, the problem is usually in the higher switch layers (a congested or mis-cabled spine), which the provider has to fix.

10. What bring-up found

Node life cycle

📦NewDelivered, inventoried
🧪TestingBurn-in, links, pairs
✅AcceptedBaseline numbers recorded
🏃In serviceHanded to the scheduler
🅿️ParkedFailed a test; fixed, then back to Testing

A repaired node always goes back to Testing, never straight into service.

Scenario
  • Across 128 nodes, bring-up parks 9 nodes: 3 with GPUs failing DCGM memory tests, 2 with a fabric port trained at reduced speed (a reseated optic fixes one, a replaced cable the other), 1 with a NIC in the wrong PCIe slot after a repair, 2 with an older firmware version, and 1 that throttles under the 24-hour burn because of a blocked airflow path.
    • All are fixed or replaced by the provider within the contract's replacement window.
    • These counts are made up for the story; Meta's real record (section 2) shows the kind of mix to expect, not the number.

Two practices make this manageable for one person:

  • One state per node: new → testing → accepted → in service, or parked with a reason. A spreadsheet works; Part 7 moves it into the scheduler's drain reasons.
  • Never repair in place: a fixed node goes back to "testing" and runs the full burn-in again. Many second failures come from the repair itself.

11. Testing storage before the run depends on it

  • Checkpoints are the main storage load of a training run: every node writes its share of model and optimiser state at the same moment.
    • If storage cannot absorb it, all 1,024 GPUs wait.
    • Gopala tests the parallel file system with the standard tools fio and IOR, from all nodes at once, writing files of the size a checkpoint shard will have, and records three numbers: aggregate write bandwidth, time to write one full checkpoint, and read bandwidth for a restart (which matters just as much, because a restart reads everything back).
  • He also checks the slow path: what happens to bandwidth when one storage server is taken out of service, because that is exactly the condition under which he will be restarting after a failure.
    • The checkpoint size itself is decided in Part 9; the policy of how often to save is in Part 7.

12. Firmware: when to upgrade, and when not to

  • Meta's Llama 3 paper notes that a number of its planned interruptions were firmware upgrades, and the site's bring-up article describes how much of the work at hyperscale is firmware.

Gopala's rules for a 128-node cluster:

  • One golden version of every firmware, recorded with the image.
  • Upgrade only for a known problem or a security fix, never because a new version exists.
  • Upgrade 4 nodes, run the full burn-in on them, run a 2-day job on them, then roll out in batches between jobs.
  • No upgrades from month 8 to the end of the main run.

13. The golden image

  • Every accepted node runs the same software image: OS, kernel, GPU driver, CUDA, NCCL, fabric drivers, DCGM, container runtime.
    • Versions are pinned and recorded, and a node whose versions differ is treated as untested.
    • Gopala keeps the image definition in git alongside his training code, so a later bug can always be traced to the exact versions it ran on.
    • Upgrades happen in a rolling way on a few nodes first, and never during the main run (the same freeze as Part 5).

14. Handing over to the scheduler

  • Bring-up ends when every accepted node is handed to the cluster software with three things attached: its baseline numbers (bandwidths, temperatures, step time on a reference job), its firmware and image versions, and its history (which tests it failed and what was replaced).
    • Part 7's health checks compare live readings with those baselines, so "node 57 is slow"
      • becomes "node 57 is 6% slower than it was on day zero", which is actionable.

15. Six bring-up mistakes

  1. Running only the full-cluster test, which says the cluster is slow but not where.
  2. Accepting nodes that passed a short diagnostic but never ran under sustained load.
  3. Putting repaired nodes straight back into service without the full burn-in.
  4. Letting firmware versions drift because each repair brought a different part.
  5. Not testing storage restart reads, only writes.
  6. Keeping results in chat threads instead of one file per node.

16. The acceptance report

  • The report that starts billing is a short table, generated from the logs: per node, the serial numbers, firmware versions, DCGM result, burn-in result, link count and speed, and pair bandwidth; then the full-cluster all-reduce result, the storage test and the 72-hour job.
    • The provider signs it too.
    • It becomes the baseline: whenever a node misbehaves later, Part 7's health checks compare it with its own day-zero numbers.

19. The series

The Maestro: 18 parts in five phases

Verdict
  • Day zero is about distrust: every node is tested alone, every link in pairs, the whole fabric together, and only then accepted and billed.
    • The parked nodes are the ones that would have stopped the run.
    • Next, Part 7: the software that keeps 1,024 GPUs busy and catches failures on its own.
